en: Verses on the Pure Land by Chan Master Puren Song of Tianting in Pilu.
Respectfully recorded by the junior disciple Derun.
Our Buddha, the Great Vow-King of Compassion, exhorts people to recite the Buddha’s name to go to the Western Land, so as to escape the cycle of rebirth within this Sahā world.

Suffering! In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the lifespan is long. If one holds the Name for seven days with an undistracted mind, the six sense faculties will become pure and their nature will shine forth brilliantly.
The Tathāgata points directly to the path of Bodhi; every word and phrase is clearly explained in the sacred scriptures.
The purification of the Buddha-land is wondrous and inexhaustible; the Palace of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with the seven treasures.

Everywhere, *kalaviṅka* birds perform before one, while pairs of peacocks dance within the groves. The opening of the superior lotuses is beyond compare, and the blossoming of their subtle fragrance is unlike any other.
While all Buddha-fields are equally adorned, none possess the exquisite ingenuity of the Pure Land.

A single thought of Suchness is present before one’s eyes; every utterance of the Buddha’s name enters the field of the mind. Contemplating the sutras to understand their meaning is the substance of the three vehicles;

reciting the Buddha’s name cultivates the lotus of the nine grades. Both essence and function, harmony and centrality, are all the self-nature; doubts are dispelled, anxieties stilled, and clinging to conditions severed.
One should maintain the name through mindfulness in this way, so that the precious raft may always rest upon the shore of the sea of suffering.
The wondrous realms of the West are sublime beyond measure; upon entering the Pure Land, one’s own mind is naturally revealed. Within the pond of eight virtues, there are lotuses of the nine grades;
within a single flower lies the Dharma in three chapters. Golden sand is spread upon the ground, azure clouds form the walls, agate stones pave the steps, and white jade forms the ramparts.
The palaces and halls are so numerous they cannot all be described; with single-minded devotion, recite the Buddha’s name and reach the Lotus Land.

Upon reaching one’s native land, the heart reveals itself; a gentle breeze stirs the fragrance of wondrous lotuses. All sentient beings possess the adamantine body; all virtues are none other than the light of wisdom.
On the rows of trees, branch after branch displays crimson and white; on the clusters of blossoms, flower after flower manifests green and yellow.
If you, sirs, can attend this Lotus Pond Assembly, you shall not leave the Master busy all day long.
Turning back from worldly affairs, enter the Dharma Hall; with steadfast resolve, recite the Buddha’s name and go to the Western Land. When you lift your head, all is the Golden Palace;
wherever you cast your eyes, nothing is not the White Jade Hall. In the Seven Treasures’ Jasper Pond, lotuses bloom; in the Water of Eight Virtues, mandarin ducks play.
O friends, when you truly arrive in the Land of Lotus, I pray you, let those who share this understanding join me in chanting this verse.

Within the presence or absence of every utterance of the Buddha’s name, it is simply that the practitioner must be filled with faith and aspiration. Through the power of aspiration, one strikes open Maitreya’s tower;
through the root of faith, one ascends to the peak of Mount Sumeru. At the treetop of Sudhana, the bright moon lingers; by the side of the Dragon Girl’s flowers, a fine breeze is sent.
Having awakened and entered the true land of the Lotus Paradise, one finally knows that the bliss of the Pure Land is inexhaustible.
This body is but a stinking leather bag; why do you cling to it and fail to think of your true home? The boundless sins committed in this life will inevitably bring retribution in future cycles.
If you are willing to turn your mind and cultivate the Pure Land, you will clearly realize the Dharma-nature and board the Compassionate Vessel.
Once the karmic consciousness within your breast is entirely eliminated, you shall behold Amitābha, the Great King of Vows, face to face.
If you intend to ascend to the Ultimate Land of Sukhāvatī, yet find no affinity with any of the Buddhas;

if your karmic consciousness from many lifetimes flows like a stream, and your afflictions from successive kalpas are as hard as iron—then, being able to realize that there is not a single thing within your breast, why need you worry or regret past transgressions?
I urge you to take up the recitation of Amitābha’s name early, lest the sovereign of your mind be dragged away by karma.
An ancient mirror from many years past requires the effort of polishing; only when grime is exhausted and dust is cleared does it begin to reflect clearly.
When stillness is cast into the midst of distracted thoughts, the chaotic mind entirely enters the tranquil heart. Deeply self-aware, one returns to the Lotus Land;
naturally and simply, one illuminates the silent void. The whole body is the Truth without obstruction—whether south, north, west, or east.
From the outset, Chan and Pure Land have never been two separate gates; there is no need to debate their distinctions. Chan returns to the Pure Land as they share the same essence;

entering the Pure Land through the Chan mind, they originate from the same source. Wondrously harmonizing with True Suchness, they constitute the Dharma-nature; those of profound capacity reach the Jeta Grove through understanding and discourse.
I urge you not to contend over self and others, but to recite the name of Amitābha to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Some say the Western Land lies before one's eyes; you must know that the Pure Land is separated from us by heaven and earth. Cease generating conceptual distinctions from within words;

the essential point lies in liberating the mind from the entanglements of suffering. When the five aggregates are searched until they are empty, the thousand Buddha-lands are revealed; when the six sense faculties are washed away, the four dhyāna heavens are transcended.
One must constantly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha; when recitation reaches the state of no-mind, one is naturally refreshed and serene.
Body forgotten, mindfulness stilled, the outflows are about to melt away; sitting upright in vast stillness, I face the azure peaks. All phenomena vanish and the mind is sovereign;
untouched by a single speck of dust, the flower of its nature is lush. Now I have first entered the realm of the Lotus Land; one day returning to the West, I shall behold the Jade Countenance.
I address my fellow practitioners and virtuous friends: news from the Lotus Land is easy to encounter.
A single lamp brightens a dark room for many years; both light and darkness arise from the mind-ground. When the eye of wisdom opens wide, ten thousand miles are unified;
when the Dharma-body has not yet manifested, the night remains obscured. It is only because of delusion that the dusty mind stagnates;
when awakening is realized, the Buddha-nature flourishes. Relying on this radiance, one returns to the Pure Land, traveling westward with ease and sovereignty.
Doubting and lacking faith, one loses the treasures of the home; willingly remaining in the Sahā world, one creates the causes for further karma.

Failing to recognize the root of suffering, which is like spreading vines, how could one know that the view of self is like misty dust? If one can simply repent for past deeds, one will reach the final ferry to the Lotus Land.
Once the mind is emptied, one passes the imperial examination; even Amitābha is but one among those who have attained this.

Delusive thoughts are endless; when will they ever cease? It requires nothing more than listening with the ears while seeking within the thoughts. When every sound meets with obstruction, there is originally no obstruction;
when every phrase returns as a flow, it ultimately does not flow. Sweep away all phenomena and return to the ground of reality;

do not, in your initial resolve, merely practice empty formalities. By turning the hearing back toward oneself, Amitābha appears; when one reaches the state of thoughtlessness, one attains liberation.
Every phrase seeks the emptiness of delusion; within that emptiness of delusion, one beholds the true master. At the first sound, all enters stillness; with every sound, there is stillness.
When one dharma is penetrated, all dharmas are penetrated. Do not say that the faculties and objects are easy to uproot; you must know that deluded thoughts are most difficult to attack.
Relying solely on the three powers of faith, vow, and practice, sweep away all mundane sentiments and the nature will naturally harmonize.
The cycles of kalpas are most tragic; there is no way to escape suffering like the Land of Ultimate Bliss. By single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha, one leaves this world;

by diligently upholding the Buddha’s name, one enters the Lotus Realm. Amidst the shadows of red banners lie the karmic debts of past lives; within the thicket of white blades lies the calamity of future rebirths.
I vow that in this life I shall return to the Pure Land, forever departing from the fires of war to go to the West.
The incessant arising and ceasing is true birth and death; day and night they attack one another like being scorched by fire. It lies right before one’s eyes, yet there is no way to resolve it.
How can one directly and forever eliminate transgressions? Simply hold the Buddha’s name and the dust of worldly toil will cease;
focus single-mindedly on Amitābha and delusions will naturally vanish. There is no need to seek any other secret or subtle method; it requires nothing more than a single resolute thought.
The thought of the sound penetrates directly back to before birth; there is no need for the heavy emotions of a boat descending into the water.

With the single phrase "Amitābha" constantly uninterrupted, the six sense-faculties are liberated and one naturally forgets the passing years. Caoxi spoke only of the mind having no abiding place; Sengzhao discussed only that things do not shift.
Grasp the subtle and wondrous principle within these, and you shall immediately ascend the lotus flower in the Jade Pond of the Nine Grades.
Arising and ceasing, the dust of worldly toil—this is the yakṣa. Why do you not sprout the bud of Bodhi? Let the field of the mind not grow the weeds of ignorance;

let the ground of nature always bloom with the flowers of wisdom. A single phrase of Amitābha is as clear as a mirror; yet the six gates, failing to maintain their guard, are as chaotic as tangled hemp.
I urge you to turn your head and look back early; the bitter sea flows on, vast and without end.
A single lamp illuminates solitude; free from worry and care, one passes the final watch of night. Let others bid farewell to the old year and its harvest;
do not concern yourself with welcoming the New Year or celebrating the dawn. With every phrase, recite the name of Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara;
with every thought, chant the Buddha’s name to transcend all worldly clamor. If one can realize the Dharma within this, a finger-snap away is the path to the Lotus Land.
I once studied the non-dual Chan of the Gate of the Patriarchs; now, wherever I go, I find a place to rest. I am ashamed that my shallow understanding lacks the virtue of a true monk;

who can accompany me in this profound mind to sleep beside the Buddha? The sound of the wind has not yet ceased as I listen through the night, while the auspicious snow is already seen falling across the heavens.
At this moment, the wind and snow arise from within the mind; thus I contemplate the realm of non-arising, which never shifts.
The layman Jinghan loves to practice Chan meditation; he has first established the karmic affinity for the Pure Land of Lotus.

Once the mind is empty and one passes the imperial examination, what prevents the nature of the Dharma from benefiting humans and devas? Through words, the principle of the True and Constant Way is revealed; having caught the rabbit, one forgets the trap, and the moon is perfectly full.
As the conversation reaches its depths, time has long passed; one completely forgets eating, drinking, and sleep.
In all matters, remain peaceful and pure in heart; fame, office, wealth, and honor do not depend on others. A dragon is no mere creature of the pond;
fine flavors have always been the treasures upon the banquet table. Every word of Amitābha can transform the multitudes; every utterance of the Buddha’s name ferries one across the ford of delusion.
As an official, let your integrity and virtue be as clear as a mirror; when you achieve your aspirations, return home to cultivate the causes of purity.
Those who contemplate the phrases of Amitābha are rare; they deeply understand the wondrous principle most subtle and profound. Amidst stillness, the Buddha-name merges with the three realms;
holding the name within the mind, one transcends all hundredfold errors. Through faith and understanding, one constantly beholds Avalokiteśvara;
in every place of practice, one perceives the profound mechanism. Pure light penetrates directly to the Land of No-Birth, illuminating Amitābha as he returns with the moon.
Originally there is neither realization nor cultivation; there is no need to single-mindedly seek outward. Recollect Amitābha until the bottom is clear;
by turning back to hear the Buddha’s name, one naturally finds ease. The six sense-faculties remain unmoving and ever tranquil; as all dharmas return to their source, everything comes to rest.
Cast aside the worldly affairs of fame and profit, and with a single mind, suddenly enter the lotus boat of the nine realms.

Dust-like thoughts cleared and tranquil, one illumines both form and emptiness. The mind is neither internal, nor external, nor in between. To have nothing upon which to dwell is called the Lotus Land;
yet the slightest speck of dust is termed the wind of objective realms. Do not say that the Pure Land is easily reached; you must know that deluded thoughts are most difficult to exhaust.
If you can let go of the faculties and consciousness, then through sincere mindfulness of Amitābha, your nature will naturally merge with it.

The eminent physician guides and transforms beings according to their causes; for those suffering from the disease of cold-fever, anger must first be avoided. With deep and subtle knowledge of the pulse’s principles, he can harmonize one's nature;
with refined and precise prescriptions, he ferries the lost across the ford. When pure perception penetrates the Dharma of purity, turbid thoughts become sparse and pure mindfulness becomes constant.
Seeing through all things as nothing but dreams and illusions, it is better to recite the Buddha’s name to repay one’s parents.
Guard against the succession of delusive thoughts at every moment; you must urgently recite the Buddha’s name to go to the Western Land.

Let the faculty of the tongue no longer produce the sufferings of Saṃsāra, and let the nostrils constantly smell the fragrance of Sukhāvatī. With one phrase of Amitābha, transcend the ocean of consciousness;
with the six faculties stilled, enter the compassionate vessel. Suddenly looking back, see all as clear as the moon; having attained this realization, wander at ease and return to your native home.
Reciting the name of Amitābha, the power of the Way is strong; the chaotic consciousnesses of karma are transformed into goodness.

Were it not for the clear reflection of the moon in the cold pond, how could the dust of defilement be extinguished so that the ultimate reality is revealed? Simply cultivate the Pure Land within this very mind; do not seek the Western Paradise elsewhere.
Practice with single-minded resolve without regressing, and day and night, throughout the six periods, you shall ever be auspicious.
The Dharma-gate of the Pure Land runs contrary to worldly ways. Do not compare its pure moon with former errors. Diligently uphold the Buddha-name, the path of true permanence;

sincerely recite Amitābha’s name, and delusions will naturally thin away. Once the six sense-faculties achieve liberation, one clearly realizes that the four marks of existence are severed from all clinging and dependence.
When merit is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled within the principle of suchness, this is precisely "passing the examination for the emptiness of mind and returning home."

Incense burned at dawn and dusk is like the pure lotus; yet delusive thoughts are difficult to eliminate, and obstacles manifest before one. If the dust of the mind is not swept away, all is but illusion;

even the clear realization of the nature-ground is no more than the state of an immortal. In suchness, one ultimately forgets what lies beyond the self; in stillness, one dwells upon the shore of the other side.
May I but suddenly transcend to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where a single point of numinous light illumines the field of the heart.
When the mind is still, one constantly perceives wondrous fragrances; why labor with the nostrils to deliberate? All manner of delusive thoughts return to the Lotus Land;
myriad dharmas and worldly conditions enter one’s native home. Do not say that the clear pool lacks Buddha-nature; you must know that the bright moon shines upon the Mind-King.
A single recitation of the Buddha’s name is like flowing water; it allows one to personally behold Amitābha, manifesting beyond all measure.

Holding fast to the Name is most appropriate; every phrase proclaims that Amitābha is one’s true home. Once you realize that the six sense-faculties are all illusions, you will understand that the four great elements are likewise impermanent.
With single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, subject and object are severed; when the five eyes are clear, they manifest with ultimate clarity.
I universally exhort you all to cultivate true mindfulness, to utterly eliminate the six thieves, and to pay homage to the King of Emptiness.
Sitting alone, my mind becomes clear and naturally expansive; letting go of all external conditions, I find joy in this secluded dwelling.

The bright moon by the window is my lotus friend; the pure breeze outside the door is my companion. A single phrase of Amitābha remains eternally tranquil; throughout the six periods of the day, the Buddha’s name is recited with spontaneous ease.
If you wish to know the true message of nianfo, maintain the name within stillness and let it illuminate the great void.

Serving as an official, do not let it hinder your mindfulness of Amitābha; when Amitābha is remembered, the myriad things are in harmony. The crane transforms into an immortal and the people enjoy their vocations;
the snake is struck and the anomalies vanish as they bathe in the waves of grace. Clearly, all this is the intent of the Lotus Land; everywhere is nothing other than the lotus of the Pure Land.
When the time arrives and the principle is revealed, weary anxieties cease; together we shall ascend to the other shore and depart from Saṃsāra.
Though the eye of wisdom is clear, its nature remains unopened; In constant delusion and inversion, one stirs up the dust and grime. The wondrous phrases within the mind flow like a stream;
Searching for them with the brush is like a swift thunderclap. Cao Mengde sang his drunken song at Chibi; Zhang Song, upon merely glancing over it, was likewise a man of rare talent.
Where now are the power and influence of these two lords? Their legacy becomes a source of laughter for later generations—how truly bitter!
Wisdom is the clever and sharp demon; I urge you to recite Amitābha’s name early. To deliberate on composing verses is a den of worldly toil;

to speculate while seeking out texts is a nest of birth and death. When the mind is swept clean until nothing remains, and the inner intent is searched until the "three many" are severed, every single thing is the realm of the Lotus Land. I ask you all, do you understand?
The realm of suffering is clearly manifest before one’s eyes; there is no need to seek answers from immortals elsewhere. With every utterance of the Buddha’s name, one escapes the calamities of war;

with every phrase of Amitābha’s invocation, one turns toward the source. Within, there is pure emptiness containing the moon of the true nature; without, no worldly dust reaches the field of the mind.
Though hundreds of thousands of demons and afflictions submit to the sovereign transformation, one must remain even firmer in reciting the name of Amitābha.
The non-Buddhists and Pāpīyān are deluded regarding right mindfulness; all this is due to their ignorance of Bodhi in past lives.

If one can know that the nature-ground contains no other things, how could it be obstructed by the field of the mind sinking into the mire? The square inch of the heart is fundamentally free from the laws of birth and extinction; how could perfect penetration be hindered by the scrutiny of "is" and "is not"?
If you instead branch off onto paths outside the essential point, you will continue as before to dwell in the bitter sea of worldly toil.
The idle person with nothing to do recites the name of Amitābha; Through this thorough recitation, they emerge from the net of suffering.

In every action and deed there is no dwelling or attachment; At every turn, the workings of transformation are naturally in harmony. The perfect light penetrates directly through to samādhi; They are welcomed into the Lotus Land in a single kṣaṇa.
Having attained this realization, they return peacefully to Sukhāvatī; How lamentable that those who do not believe—what can be done for them?
Monks practicing nianfo, do not lightly abandon it. When reciting the name of Amitābha, know who it is that knows.
Once you have thoroughly awakened to the field of the mind, there will be no obstructions; when you clearly realize the nature-ground, what more remains to be done?
Singing the song of Suchness in Sanskrit sounds, adorning it with silent words in the Han language—if the mind wanders into conventional truth, then beneath the *kāṣāya* one wears only feathers.
The cultivation of the Daoist school centers on the *dantian*. When the mind is directed toward the furnace, it becomes exceptionally firm.
To know the true elixir of longevity that never ages, one must understand that within the furnace there is no dust or smoke. The islands of Penglai in the sea are ultimately not eternal;
the Land of Ultimate Bliss is a realm of carefree and sovereign freedom. I respectfully advise the Daoist masters to recite the Buddha’s name; there is no need to seek immortals elsewhere.
The *niṣīdana* reminds one to keep the mind firm in mindfulness of the Buddha. Those from wealthy and noble families seldom go to wear it; sitting and guarding the empty gate, the mind is at ease.

Dwelling in a quiet chamber, the jewel of one’s nature becomes perfect. With a single recitation of the Buddha’s name, the Lotus Land is near; when the myriad dharmas are all extinguished, one is in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
When birth and death confront you like a dream or an illusion, rely solely on the power of the Buddha to enter the lotus pond.

Young man, do not harbor doubts when reciting the Buddha’s name; this single phrase of Amitābha is the foundation for transcending the world. When birth and death arrive, there is neither old nor young;

how could right and wrong avail anything when the *maṇi* jewel is missing? Prepare your provisions and expenses in advance while alive; then, after you depart, they will naturally suffice without deficiency.
Do not wait until the last moment to "climb on the Buddha’s feet"; once life has ended, regret can no longer be remedied.
In old age, recite the Buddha’s name to go to the Western Land; Cast aside all worldly attachments and strengthen your resolve. Each word of Amitābha must be practiced with sincerity;
With every utterance of the Buddha’s name, do not engage in discursive thought. Advancing years are like a candle before the wind; Passing days are like frost upon a tile.
When the moment of birth and death arrives, rely on the Buddha’s power; With single-minded focus and no duality, enter the Lotus Land.
For the sick person, mindfulness of the Buddha is the excellent remedy. Amidst intense suffering, do not become disordered or frantic.

When not a single thought arises, the whole body is revealed; when the six sense organs stir, that is the Demon King. At all times, diligently sweep away delusive thoughts; day after day, never forget Amitābha.
By reciting his name, the various illnesses within the heart will retreat; the flower will bloom and the Buddha be seen, with a lifespan beyond measure.
When death approaches, the body is beyond all things; first, one must recognize the person of original nature. This skin-sack will not last long;
how could this mass of blood and sinews be the true self? On the vast and boundless path ahead, one must recite the Buddha’s name; with feet firmly planted, one emerges from the ford of delusion.
In the land of the Lotus Paradise, there is no birth or extinction; casting off the hand, one returns to the West to meet one’s old kin.
How truly pitiable are the ignorant! Within their chests, no wisdom has been cultivated, but only heaps of karma. In past lives, they slandered the path to the Lotus Land;
in this life, they enter the womb of suffering in blindness. Do not say that the cycle of rebirth carries no retribution; know that one must now suffer the calamities of ignorance.
If you can reform and abandon your former deeds, reciting the name of Amitābha will cause that karma to be consumed like ash.
The foolish person dreams of being enfeoffed as a marquis; they brood all day long and suffer all day long.

Like flour mixed with oil that cannot be separated, or like a moth flying into a flame that burns its own head, their mental field is blind and dull due to karma from past lives. Because their fundamental nature remains unenlightened, they have no desire to practice.
If you would only turn back and direct your heart toward the good, recite the Buddha’s name and repent for your transgressions.
Sentient beings tormented by suffering commit many deeds; life after life, they fall into the river of the underworld. When one body commits a sin, none are not one's own;

before the judgment seats of the Ten Halls, each is but oneself. With horse-faced demons brandishing pitchforks, the heart is filled with dread; with ox-headed demons holding halberds, what can one do?
Turn the mind and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha; in the space of a finger-snap, one escapes the net.
Pleasure is the cause of suffering for sentient beings; guard against the six thieves with vigilance. A single invocation of the Buddha’s name is the Way;
the four-character name of Amitābha is the stainless body. The Dharma-body is fundamentally without pleasure or pain; how could True Suchness ever undergo sinking and delusion?
When you realize the meaning of the Lotus Land in the future, you will finally believe that your previous efforts were a mistaken path.
The afflictions do not arise, for originally there is nothing; yet alas, sentient beings cling with great persistence. They fall into the root of doubt like spreading vines;
wherever a thought stirs, it is like wind and waves. If the principle of true emptiness is not realized within the breast, one will constantly seek a dwelling of self-mastery within the heart.
To desire to attain the Land of Ultimate Bliss through external forms is like spending a lifetime in the dream of Nanke.
In practicing mindfulness of the Buddha, let it be constant within the mind. Alas for sentient beings, their consciousness is frantic with karmic activity;

as soon as they wish to recite the single phrase of Amitābha, the six sense-faculties stir in disorder and they fall into madness. They have counted the national treasures of others, yet they refuse to regard them as their own family jewels.
Practicing in such a manner, one exerts effort in vain, for one does not know that the spiritual radiance lies within the foundations of mindfulness.

Amitābha Buddha is the Great Physician King; he receives and guides deluded beings back to their native home. When recitation reaches the state where the mind is empty, one attains the highest degree;
both sentient beings and Buddha are forgotten together. Holding the name inherently does not fall into conceptual calculation; reciting the Buddha’s name is like the light of the bright moon.
Upon thorough awakening, there is only this single phrase before you; there is no need to inquire about the Western Paradise at the end.
While walking, recite the Buddha’s name without delay; within that mindfulness, polish Amitābha until he is bright and clear. Your feet shall tread upon the true ground of the Lotus Land;
your mind, holding the Buddha’s name, shall sweep away the hosts of demons. At every turn, the realm of the West appears; at every step, there is nothing but the lotus flowers of Sukhāvatī.
Now, relying on the faculty of faith and the power of aspiration, ascend early to the Pure Land and depart from this Saha world.

While dwelling [in this state], recollect the Buddha without indistinctness. Among the four great elements, who is "I"? When mindfulness is forgotten and both [subject and object] are extinguished, the waves of the mind are stilled;
as soon as the root of consciousness moves, the illusory winds call forth. Not a single speck of dust is established, for the source is originally empty and still;

the myriad dharmas, in their ultimate penetration, are neither existent nor non-existent. If you can realize this within, you possess true sovereignty; you will personally arrive at the Pure Land and receive the consecration of the clarified butter.
When sitting, contemplate the Buddha; do not covet sleep. With every phrase, Amitābha Buddha appears before you. In the center of the Eight Virtues Pond, the mind is sovereign;

atop the Nine Lotus Platforms, the nature is eternally perfect. When observing while sitting that there is no Buddha, only then is one called a Buddha; when listening in stillness that there is no immortal, only then is one truly an immortal.
If within this state you err by even a hair’s breadth regarding Buddha and immortal, worldly toil will once again surge like a surging tide across the heavens.
When lying down, mindfulness of the Buddha is most refreshing; within each breath, one creates a dharma-pavilion.

Though the soiled garments upon the body have not yet been removed, the tranquil realm within the breast enters the Lotus Land. Upon awakening, one realizes the vastness of the blue sky; forgotten is the white moonlight of the third watch.
I exhort you all to diligently recite the Buddha’s name, together ascending to the other shore to pay homage to the Mind-King.
Wealth comes from the accumulation of hidden merit by one’s ancestors; in all matters, harmony ensures the flow of one’s spirit.

There has never been a family wealthy for a thousand years in this world, nor has there ever been a person poor for a hundred years among men. Where are the Six States now that Qin swallowed them? Even the Three Qi obtained by Han is but empty.
Simply recite the name of Amitābha to return to the Pure Land; the source of wealth there far surpasses the prosperity of this world.
O Immortal of Peace and Bliss in this Sahā world of wealth and honor, with lofty gates and manifest doors, you stand as my companion.
Having planted the seeds of Bodhi over many lifetimes, the glory and splendor of this present life have naturally ripened as fruit. Yet, alas, this mundane body will not endure forever;

how much better it would be to recite the Buddha’s name and enter the lotus of the Pure Land. In the West, one attains an eternally living body, far surpassing the heavens of this turbid Jambudvīpa world.
The poor are truly pitiable; they lack even three meals of tea and rice. Searching the home through, what millet remains? Washing the waist-pouch clean, not a half-cash is left.
Not having cultivated merit in past lives, one suffers now in the present. If you practice goodness in this life, it will become the cause for future blessings.
It takes nothing more than to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha; naturally, there will be superior lotus flowers to satisfy your hunger.
If those of low station err for even a single thought, they shall not obtain the sprouts of a favorable cause in this life.
The scribe busily carries firewood and rice; the handmaid busily boils tea. If one can only diligently recite the Buddha’s name within the breast, then the Bodhi flower will bloom in the heart.
At all times, do not let the name of Amitābha be obscured; with a single thought of returning the light, one reaches the ancestral home.

In his official writings, his brushwork possesses divine power; the ingenuity within his breast is all due to past causes. Who could have foreseen that he would pass the imperial examinations in consecutive years?
With a single success, he became a minister of state. In former times, he opened up profit from turbid waters; now, he brings glory to those who study the classics.
Though such high status and renown must eventually end, it is better to maintain one’s name and recognize one’s old kin.
The farmer’s recitation of the Buddha’s name is most distinct: with both hands holding seedlings, he walks backward. Every phrase of the *Namu Amida Butsu* is practiced with sincerity;
every sound of the Buddha’s name gives rise to pure causes. Others have no ground of their own and drift with the wind; I have a field of the heart where I plow under the moon.
Year after year, there is hope for the provisions of sustenance; throughout the four seasons, there is joy in peace and harmony.
Craftsmanship is refined and the mind is most subtle; the seal is impressed upon the hands with ease. To carve dragons, one must rely on the power of grasping the clouds;

to engrave phoenixes, one must depend on the mechanism of fishing for the moon. All matters are clear and bright, yielding skill as it follows; yet all manner of techniques are ultimately illusory and not real.
It is better to lay down the karma of worldly toil and recite the name of Amitābha, returning with the moon.

The merchant seeks wealth with high spirits, yet his household affairs have weathered the winds and frost. Trading in all directions, he leaves his native land; piling gold from every side, he dwells in a distant realm.
When profit is great, one must guard against the perils of wind and waves; when wealth is abundant, it is hard to avoid injury from thieves.
There is no better way than to diligently recite the name of Amitābha Buddha; then the bright pearl within one’s robe will shine forth of its own accord.
The fisherman profits when the net covers all the boats; morning and night he never stops lowering his hook.
Under the fine, misty rain by the willow banks, the cold wind blows across the reed islands. Though gaining profit before one’s eyes may seem good, I fear that later Yama will not let him rest.
Failing at the end despite facing the Three Heavens above, it would be better to recite the Buddha’s name and turn back early.
The woodcutter’s mindfulness of the Buddha grows even firmer; With every word of Amitābha, years pass unnoticed.

Wild grasses and falling flowers after the cold rain, Idle clouds and wild cranes at the edge of the setting sun. Lush before the crags is the realm of the West; Vibrant green beyond the mountains is the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
If one recognizes the true Pure Land within this, Amitābha will welcome them into the lotus pond.
Tilling the soil and reading from the heart-field, one must look toward the ancients; when the farmer attains his livelihood, he dwells in peace and ease.
The cowherd boy lies at his ease by the flowers; the water-buffalo sleeps carefree upon the grass. When the five grains ripen in abundance, the people delight in their work;
through song and dance in the four seasons, they celebrate the reign of Yao. May everyone together recite the name of Amitābha Buddha, and hand-in-hand ascend the boat of Prajñā.
When reading books, do not seek the truth within the words; in true study, do not pursue it outside the sentences. When the fish and the rabbit are caught, one enters the Way;

what further use is there for the trap or the snare? To turn back and look is unnecessary. Saints and ordinary beings are distinct as many forms, yet the Three Teachings flow together as a single boat.
Simply recite the name of Amitābha and return to the Pure Land; let greed, anger, ignorance, and attachment all cease at once.

At dawn, during the hour of the Tiger (寅), one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha with purity. When traveling on the road, one must remain vigilant. Every sound of the Buddha’s name is the treasure of the body;
every phrase of Amitābha is the cause for transcending the world. If the luminous pearl within has not yet been penetrated, seeking a teacher externally is not the true path.
When there comes a time when both inner and outer are thoroughly clear, one will perceive Amitābha turning the wheel of Dharma.
At dawn, at the hour of the Rabbit, contemplate the Buddha; with a devout heart take refuge, do not let the moment slip away. With a single recitation, one reaches the Land of Peaceful Lotuses;

when the myriad dharmas are realized within the mind, it is the slope of the Pure Land. Everywhere is nothing other than the manifestation of one’s own nature; every single thing is a river for ferrying beings across.
Suddenly, when both mind and Buddha are extinguished together, one clearly perceives that worldly toil has emerged from the net.
At the hour of the Dragon, recite the Buddha’s name in a low voice; with every phrase, Amitābha and the Pure Land sprout forth. In the green waters, the empty mind reflects deeply;
upon the gray moss, the nature waits for the moon, ever luminous. Few among men remain unstained by a single speck of dust; all phenomena are empty, transcending worldly glory.
When the flowers of Ultimate Bliss bloom in their nine grades, may we together ascend to the other shore and realize non-arising.
At the hour of the snake, one realizes that mindfulness of the Buddha is birthless. Having realized this birthlessness, the ground of the mind becomes luminous;

it is like the moon of nature reflected in a deep pool, or like an empty valley responding to a hollow sound. It tears asunder the single flavor of the unconditioned Dharma, yet manifests ten thousand varieties of distinct names.
Do not attempt to fix the ultimate meaning within the mind; you must know that the essential requirement is to transcend both forms and emotions.
At the hour of noon, the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha dwells in the center; a single phrase of Amitābha is harmonized beyond all bounds. One must diligently sweep and cleanse one’s own person;

do not say that the path to the Pure Land is difficult to exhaust. When the chest is free of deluded thoughts, the Way of the Three Vehicles is present; when the heart possesses the sprout of spiritual wisdom, the myriad dharmas are penetrated.
In days to come, you shall personally arrive at the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where the true master will emerge from within a lotus flower.
At the hour of Wei, one recites the Buddha’s name as the sun slants toward the west. If one’s practice is not authentic, one is defiled by the mud of samsara.

Even the slightest attachment of the mind is entirely delusion; yet in its true nature, there is neither affliction nor confusion. With a single utterance of the Buddha’s name, one reaches the realm of the Lotus Land; by upholding these four characters, one dwells in the Pure Land.
When the time arrives and the principle is revealed, the true nature manifests, and all together return to Ultimate Bliss to realize Bodhi.

Recite the Buddha’s name during the hour of the Monkey (3–5 p.m. without conceptualization; as soon as one engages in thought, delusion grows stronger. When the three karmas are purely harmonious, one is always at ease;

when the six sense faculties are fully penetrating, one enters the Lotus Land. Wherever merit is perfected, it is Amitābha Buddha; in every instance where fruition is complete, he is the Great Awakened King.
Recite until non-arising is reached and the mind manifests itself naturally; like wind fanning a fire, the fragrance of the nature blossoms.
At the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), I returned to the mountain chanting the Buddha’s name. I grieved deeply for my own condition as tears flowed spontaneously. My mind was not clear and my wisdom shallow;

within my breast, obstructions and delusions were linked like a chain. If the roots of worldly dust are not uprooted, there is the suffering of saṃsāra; yet when karmic consciousness exhausts itself in emptiness, the true nature returns of its own accord.
Ceasing thought and returning to the source is the truly pure land; the white jade of the Jingshan mountains is originally free of any speck of blemish.
At the hour of the Dog, recite the Buddha’s name with clarity; you must recognize that this Sahā world is a pit of fire.

When the great limit arrives, it is truly dark; Yama does not ask about the difficult path ahead. With single-minded devotion, recite Amitābha’s name early on, so as to avoid the suffering of the moment of death.
I exhort all of you to awaken quickly; do not let yourselves fall into the blindness of regret later.
At the hour of Hai, one recites the Buddha’s name within the breast-chamber; when the night is still and deep, one contemplates one’s native land. Do not say that the Lotus Land is easily reached;
you must know that encountering circumstances leads to delusion and blindness. A single orb of bright moon shines upon the void, and ten thousand points of fading stars manifest to the very bottom.
If you recognize this, the moon of the mind appears; there is no need to laboriously seek the Western Quarter elsewhere.
At the hour of Zi, the recitation of the Buddha’s name is precisely at the third watch. Delusive thoughts are difficult to discern as they wander through day and night.
If you have deep faith in Avalokiteśvara, what need is there to worry beforehand about the arising of obstacles? A single sound of the Buddha’s name is beyond the blue heavens;
the four characters of Amitābha are as bright as the white moon. There is no need to seek other esoteric methods; it simply requires that, moment after moment, you inquire about the path home.
In the hour of the Ox, I recite the Buddha’s name while listening to the cock crow; with every phrase, I carefully evaluate Amitābha.

The drifting clouds above have all dispersed, and the solitary moon in the sky is perfectly clear. With a mindless heart, the Buddha-nature merges with the triple world; with intentional effort, one ascends beyond the five watches of the night.
Prepare your provisions early for the return to the Pure Land; you cannot dig a well when the time of need arrives.
On the Spring Equinox, one must be firm in mind while reciting the Buddha’s name. A single incense offering burns within the burner; with warm sun and fresh breezes, a new atmosphere arises.
The colors of spring are more vibrant than they were before. With every sound, chant the song of non-arising; with every phrase, uphold the conditions for the Pure Land.
By holding the four characters of the Name, one returns to Sukhāvatī—what need is there to seek another boat to ferry one across?

Rain and wind harmonize; body and function are in accord. With single-mindedness and no distraction, one departs from Saṃsāra. As ice melts and the lingering snow falls, the beauty of spring is faint;
under the warmth of the sun and the gentleness of the breeze, one contemplates the Buddha. Once the mind is free from the mark of self, all illusory traces within it are likewise consumed.
Cease seeking the extraordinary beyond the norm; even to seek the original source is itself a demon.

When thunder is heard at the awakening of insects, all things harmonize; what is the meaning of single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name? When the sense-faculties and their objects are swept away, Amitābha appears;
even the consciousness that drags one through emptiness is He. When both person and phenomena are forgotten, it is called Ultimate Bliss;

when mundane sentiments do not arise, delusions are few. Every sound of the Buddha’s name is the principle of True Suchness; entering the holy and transcending the ordinary occurs in a single instant.
Reciting the Buddha’s name is most appropriate at the spring equinox. When this moment arrives, do not distance yourself from it. As the essence of spring fades, the eyes of the willows bloom;

warmth spreads and the season for blossoms begins. Though worldly affairs remain like dust and burdens, difficult to clear away, when the principle reaches perfect integration, it is beyond all conditioned existence.
Seize this spring light to seek the path; do not greedily cling to mundane matters and lose the *maṇi* jewel.
On this Qingming season, rain-like flowers fall. To sweep the ancestral graves, one steps through the door. The wind sweeps across the riverhead where waves are treacherous;
Clouds gather by the embankment where the sounds of wailing are sparse. If ancestors wish to be reborn in the Lotus Realm, Children and grandchildren must practice with devotion and never fail.
Today is the Cold Food Festival of the Forbidden Smoke; With single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha, head westward toward rebirth.
At Grain Rain, holding the Name is like a swift clap of thunder; a single invocation of the Buddha’s name sweeps away all dust and grime.
It unties the six knots until no knot remains, and it washes clean both the ordinary and the sagely wombs. When the mind reaches a state of distraction, one must recite the Buddha’s name;
when affairs become busy, one must pull oneself back from them. If one can cultivate the Lotus Land in this way, the spiritual light will be ushered into the Jade Terrace.

As the Clear and Harmonious season begins with the start of summer, I am busy reciting the Buddha’s name. Each phrase of Amitābha’s name I personally take upon myself. From this day forth, the auspicious air of the year shall depart;
the springtime of ninety days will be revealed only after the year has passed. In this land of the East, times are often in flux; in the Lotus Realm of the West, life is immeasurable.
Only now do I realize the suffering of the cycle of deluded thoughts; I vow that in this very life I shall return to my native home.
In the season of Lesser Fullness, upholding the Name has profound significance. When not a single speck of dust remains, one attains the utmost cool serenity.

The sun hastens the Emperor of Fire as it departs, yet the air remains clear and harmonious; thus, let your mindfulness grow ever stronger. If there is dust within the heart, all is delusion; if there is nothing in the breast, one is neither blind.
I urge you to quickly make the vow for the Western Land, so that you may avoid being busily distracted by worldly toil all day long.
At芒種 (Mangzhong), farmers are busy everywhere; they never forget the single phrase of Amitābha. With bountiful harvests and damp rains, the seedlings sprout early;

with a prosperous year and gentle breezes, the awns emerge. Plowing, sowing, and weeding are ultimately bitter toil; yet the autumn reaping and winter ripening bring a measure of peace and well-being.
In this Sahā world, every year requires great effort; in the Pure Land, at all times, there is supreme auspiciousness.
On the summer solstice, one reverently contemplates the Buddha; at Tiger Creek, the distant ancestors planted lotuses. In the pond, the *phǔ* grass is green and the cool breeze scarce;

in the courtyard, the *liú* flowers are red and the heat intense. All phenomena are perfectly interfused as they return to the Pure Land; every particle of dust reaches its ultimate end upon the Lotus Slope.
This single phrase of "Amitābha Buddha" is suchness itself—when consciousness is transformed into wisdom, it is accomplished in a single instant.
During the Lesser Heat, one holds the Name with utmost sincerity; at all times, one practices within the faith of the Buddha’s name. When days are long, the lotus blossoms like the autumn moon;

when nights are short, the high paulownia tree resembles the Great Clarity. Facing objects, how could there ever be a "boundary"? Sending forth the mind, there is nowhere it does not find the glory of the heart.
Amidst purity, mindfulness of the Buddha brings constant peace and joy; every phrase of Amitābha shines with extraordinary brilliance.
The great heat flows like molten gold, as if struck by fire; not a trace of warmth reaches the heart. Let the Red Emperor’s solar disk stand at its zenith;

heed not the fierce majesty of the golden bird. With the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu," one is ever free; through reciting the Buddha’s name throughout the six periods, one realizes perfect penetration.
If you wish to know the true message within, it is the same everywhere when the seasons turn to autumn.
Autumn begins; as I recite the Buddha’s name, the blazing heat turns back. Jade dew and golden winds urge on every passing moment. The moonlight grows faint as the Three Fruits end;
The autumn light deepens with a single roll of thunder. What is heard by the ear is unreal—originally not suffering; What is seen by the eye is dustless—the mind naturally turns to ash.
Heat departs and cold arrives—all is an illusion. Having clearly realized the nature of the mind, one enters the lotus womb.
As the heat subsides and autumn arrives, the Way grows easier to cultivate. At the six periods of the day, recite the Buddha’s name with even greater devotion.
The cicadas chirp and the birds clamor; the mountains remain verdant and the waters remain clear. When the time comes, the principle is revealed and self-centered views are forgotten.
Through perfect integration and liberation, all mundane attachments are ended. The Western Pure Land is called "Blissful"; simply recite Amitābha’s name with diligent steps.
Holding the Name amidst white dew, one is deluded and frantic; reflecting on it again and again, the name becomes manifest and renowned.

One must know that the suffering of saṃsāra is but a dust-like illusion, and that this physical body is not permanent. If you turn your heart back toward the Buddha and diligently recite His name, what need is there for anxious thought or regret over past misdeeds?
It requires only these four characters to put into practice; when the fruit is fulfilled and merit perfected, you shall return to your original home.
On the day of autumnal equinox, do not indulge in slothful sleep; one phrase of Amitābha requires firm faith. Let the mind follow the myriad phenomena as they change;

when the nature penetrates the three voids, the Pure Land is perfected. When the six gates are beyond dependence, one constantly forgets the Buddha; when the single dharma is entirely true, one does not linger in meditation.
If there is even a speck of dust that cannot be swept away, the waves of karmic consciousness will once again overflow the heavens.
In the cold dew, hold the name with mindfulness most subtle; seeking birth in the Pure Land, faith rests upon it.
Observe how last night the west wind blew fiercely, and this morning the yellow leaves fell. On all four sides, mist and clouds are all reciting the Buddha’s name;
what contradiction is there in a hundred-year life? There is no need to seek efficacy elsewhere; simply recite Amitābha, for delusions will naturally thin away.
When the frost descends and one holds fast to the Name, all affairs come to rest. Time passes swiftly once again as autumn wanes. The golden wind blows down the leaves of the *wutong* tree;

the cold moon shines upon the empty ground and the ox. When the essence of reality is opened wide, heaven and earth are still; the spiritual mechanism is penetrated and transcended—there is no need to seek it elsewhere.
When even a mote of dust is stripped away, Amitābha appears; only then does one reach the further shore of the Lotus Land.
On the commencement of winter, I recite the Buddha’s name by your side; the meaning of this single phrase of Amitābha is fragrant.

The days are short and worldly affairs are few, the nights are long and tranquil, and the resolve for the Way grows strong. Within the home lies the very chamber of the Lotus Land; beyond material things, how could there not be the field of the Pure Land?
When you reach the other shore, I pray you turn your gaze back toward the incense; Amitābha is, in fact, manifested within one's own nature.
On a light snow day, one holds the Name facing west; when the cold wind enters the mouth, the breath is difficult to sustain.
Recite the phrase "Namu Amitābha Buddha" deeply, and even a shallow recitation can lead one to dwell in the Pure Land. Within, there is the Jade Pond containing the moon of nature;

without, there are no worldly affairs, so one forgets the tracks of the hoof. If a person can understand this inner meaning, they will realize that the lotus land is like a moon reflecting in a mountain stream.

When the great snow and cold arrive, reciting the Buddha’s name brings peace; with each invocation of the Buddha’s name, there is a sound of joy. Seeking plum blossoms while treading through the snow is one's own personal affair;

boiling tea while striking the ice is likewise no difficulty. While life and death remain unclarified, constantly recite the Buddha’s name; though right and wrong may be obscured, observe them with a mindful heart.
Suddenly, when the sun shines upon the realm of the Lotus Land, you shall arrive at that Lotus Land and sit within the precious palanquin.
At the winter solstice, yang is born, yet it grows ever colder. The sound of every Buddha-name brings peace within stillness. The wind blows, leaves fall, and the thousand mountains grow thin;

The rain beats down, thick frost falls, and the hundred grasses wither. If you can realize the true Dharma-nature within your breast, You will clearly understand the mind-ground and enter the contemplation of emptiness.
Though these are but a few ordinary words, They surpass the exquisite meaning of the three vehicles.

In Lesser Cold, mindfulness and Buddha-recitation merge as one; amidst the fine, misty rain, within the second nine days of the lunar month, every thought-moment is the perfectly luminous essence of true nature, and every sound awakens the Lord of the House. When all conditions have ceased, what trace remains?
A single point of cold light shines upon the azure sky. This is the true purport of the Lotus Land; its profound mysteries are difficult to exhaust.
In the great cold, mindfulness of the Buddha possesses spirit; the single phrase of Amitābha is ever new each day. When mindful of the Buddha, the traces of the Buddha are nowhere to be found;
when the mind is exhausted, what cause remains for its tracks? Piteous are those who turn their heads and look back; they mistakenly recognize the one who grasps the incense or embraces the fire.
If you understand the four characters within your breast, the hundred-and-eight bright pearls are your own family treasure.
The Patriarch Yongming Shou said: "To possess both Chan and Pure Land is like being a tiger with horns.
May those who study the Buddha in this world likewise practice both Chan and Pure Land as a supreme Dharma-gate.
In the autumn of the Ji-mao year, (Qingyu) and Xu Lingxu of Qiantang together carved the *Easy Explanation of Master Puan’s Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Pure Land Verses*. At that time...
Among those who cultivate pure karma, nearly every household possesses a volume, and almost every person holds a fascicle in their hand.
In the winter of that year, the venerable Gwan showed me the Dharma-talks of our teacher, Master Jingniam (Chongnim).

Upon receiving and reading them, I saw that every word pierced to the very peak and every phrase penetrated the essence; they directly point to the time before Wei-yin (the primordial ancestor), exerting power to draw one back toward it.
Regarding this final point: My Master and Master Pu were brothers in the Dharma. For many years, they respectively presided over Tianning Temple;
one extensively propagated the Pure Land teachings, while the other broadly expounded the Zen tradition.
Thus, their principles regarding Chan and Pure Land harmonized perfectly with those of Master Shou. Recalling the winter of the Jiashu year of the Tongzhi era (1874), (Qingyu).
I traveled from Taiwan to the mainland. A fierce north wind howled and the ocean waves rose like mountains; our ship encountered perilous turbulence, yet by grace we returned alive.
Hardly had I arrived at Wumen when my spirit was still unsettled, yet I immediately took a small boat to Piling to visit my teacher at his quarters in Tianning Monastery.
At that time, the teacher’s illness was already grave, yet he exerted himself to rise and confer upon me (Qingyu) the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
He exhorted [Qingyu] repeatedly with the unsurpassed path of the Buddha to encourage him. Yet, before even two weeks had passed, the Master finally entered parinirvāṇa.
(Qingyu) always grieved that his karmic affinity with his Master was so shallow, such that he could not constantly receive the Master’s staff and shouts.

Now, fortunately having obtained this compilation, he reads and recites it from time to time, contemplating and investigating it in silence. He hopes that one day his mind-ground will be vast and clear, and he may attain...
One beholds one’s original face; there is not the slightest separation from our Master within the realm of eternal quiescent light.

The Master spoke with wordlessness; [Master] Qingyu heard with non-hearing. Why, then, must one raise it in the morning and command it in the evening before being permitted to be considered one who has personally attended a man of the Way?
Hasten to entrust this to the carving blocks so that it may be widely circulated. On the day of the Master’s cremation, there was a *śarīra* (relic)...

My son (Cheong-ŭm) personally obtained one grain [of the relic] and enshrined it in the temple. Whenever all worldly conditions receded and fell silent, he would burn incense and sit in meditation, contemplating the True Body.
Like the moon reflected in water, it was luminous in its emptiness; his sense faculties and their objects were both liberated. O Master, O Master!
How could this possibly be within the reach of ordinary worldly conditions?
July, the seventh year of Guangxu. Disciple Qingyu bows his head in reverence and respectfully records this.
